speechtext: Is the hon. member aware that in the United States a married taxpayer with no dependants, with a gross income of $4,000 a year, pays $207 more in income tax?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It may well be so and if the parliamentary secretary quotes these figures to me I am quite prepared to accept his statement to that effect, but this is not the point. We are now at a certain plane where taxes have been fixed and provide a certain amount both here and in the United States, and the minister is suggesting that in order to contain inflation he must raise taxes. I do not accept that as being a proper program, and with the greater danger that exists in the United States I say that if the United States authorities felt the same way about it the President and the government of the United
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin States would also have raised taxes. It is a matter of relativity rather than comparison, Mr. Speaker.
This whole business reminds me a lot of a device which was in existence in the early days in the United Kingdom. The Prince of Wales had a boy called a whipping boy and when the prince did something wrong the whipping boy was upended and received punishment. This is exactly what is happening here. Because of the errors made by the government and certain people in industry and finance, a large minority of people in the lower income brackets are the ones who are being punished, and that is not the kind of answer which is good enough for this house.
There are other issues which ought to be raised and made the subject of discussion in any proper Budget debate. To a very large extent prices are made up by cost generated by the imposition of taxes. Certainly the values of capital and labour which go into the price of a commodity or a service are in considerable measure fixed by taxation and, especially in modern days, the pyramiding effect of taxation. Taxation in turn is fixed by the cost of government and I suggest it is hypocrisy for the government to tell labour ar.d industry to follow guide lines until it itself submits to self-discipline and puts its own house in order.
There is the mounting tide of government employees. There is the rejection and refusal to follow all but a fraction of the Glassco commission recommendations. There is the incidence of error, of waste, of extravagance and non-productive payments which are contained in the Auditor General's report, and the government has also failed to follow 80 per cent of the recommendations of the Public Accounts Committee.
It is no wonder that industry and labour reply "so what" to the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) when they very timidly suggest that they should limit their price increases and wage demands. I think they are perfectly entitled to say, "You start and we will follow." I think this is absolutely essential.
I should like to talk more about taxation but the time allowed is against me. However, there will be ample opportunity when the Carter royal commission report is brought in. But it is my submission that the present taxation system, like a crazy quilt, has been built up without rhyme or reason, without regard to the cardinal principle of an equitable tax system, namely, one which permits
April 22, 1966

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin people to have the fullest access to the resources of a country unimpaired by incentive destroying levies. I think the first essential is not an increase in taxation but a reduction, a reduction which follows a decrease in the cost of government, in the controllable cost of government expenditures with which this government has not shown the slightest intention of dealing.
On the other branch of fiscal policy, the tariff, there is the question if a policy of freer trade would not bring more goods at cheaper prices within the reach of the Canadian consumer. In this regard we must not lose sight of the psychological aspect of purchasing at the present time. One cannot call it hoarding, but there is no doubt that with the continuous talk of inflation and the learned dissertations of people about the overheating of the economy, and the grave and serious mien adopted by government people, financial editors and others, there has occurred a built-in psychotic feeling, the desire to buy something now even though one does not need it because it might not be available later or will only be available later at an increased price.
I suggest that a large amount of the purchasing taking place at the present time is because of this psychological factor.
If it were made aware to people that tariff barriers would be reduced to a limit that would permit a greater flow of goods coming into the country, a lot of this fear would be lost. I am not too concerned about labour and industry, in the sense that they are organized. My concern is with the consumer and I suggest, despite all opinions to the contrary, it is more than time that the industries which have become fat and lazy behind protection should be exposed to the cool fresh wind of competition and get out on their own.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Certainly this should be done on a staggered and progressive basis. There should be tax incentives for research development, improving techniques, and an orderly transition to the type of industrial activity where, with increasing productivity, markets can always be found at home and abroad in the face of any competition. Canadian industries with access to great and varied types of natural resources and with know-how and competence should be able to compete anywhere including their own country without the help of tariffs as they now exist. In the modern industrial age the benefits which have accrued through economy of scale now can be


matched and even surpassed by the economy of diversification and automation. This is where our destiny lies.
In this regard I should like to put before the house the bare outlines of some arguments made by others which bolster my own view. In the Toronto Telegram of April 19 I find that Mr. Douglas, the president of Douglas Aircraft Company, came to Canada and the following item appeared:
Lack of interest in subcontracting by Canadians startles Douglas chief. Canadian manufacturers have displayed a lack of interest in obtaining subcontracts from the Douglas Aircraft Company...
"Your government came down and leaned on us pretty heavily and said let's see some work in Canada"...
"But when we sent some teams up to Canada three or four years ago, people said we don't want your business."
Then, Mr. Speaker, again with reference to the Economic Council of Canada, at page 172 there is a very strong opinion to the effect that the role of Canada should be one which recognizes the growing degree of international economic interdependence. More specifically, an active and meaningful role by Canada in negotiations to broaden and deepen nondiscriminatory multilateral trade coincides with our long term interests and position as a major world trader. Putting it very shortly I suggest that freer trade, the opening up of our markets, and more and more goods and services coming in here would result in Canadian industry being compelled to become effective, efficient and demonstrate its ability to produce at lower costs. This would immediately make available not only more commodities to Canada at a cheaper price but would put us in a better competitive position with relation to the rest of the world.
I do not think it is good enough to say that because the tariffs have existed and because the Kennedy round of tariff negotiations is not proceeding as fast as it should we are not free to take action on our own. I think we are, and I would like to see this matter discussed. There are other considerations such as the question of United States capital coming into this country. There has been much opinion stated on that. I should like to refer hon. members to a book called "The Prospect of Change and Proposals for Canada's Future". This contains a number of essays by various people, some of whom are professors and even economists. One of them at page 245 is considering the effect of foreign ownership and control of Canadian industry. There a question is raised in respect
April 22, 1966

of whether there is a danger in reasonable and moderate use of foreign capital in Canada. I am not here taking sides one way or the other but I do suggest this is not a one-sided proposition and is one which should be considered. There are other considerations.
Mr. Harry Johnston, a well known Canadian economist, suggests that in his view there would be absolutely no advantage in the change suggested by the last minister of finance, that all it would do would be to pass control to James Street and Bay Street rather than Wall Street. I say that this is the sort of thing we should be discussing. There is the question of designated areas and the northern part of Canada having a tremendous potential for industrial development. This is progressing slowly because it takes risk capital. Every time I see under the designated area program the designation of certain areas to permit the continuation of an uneconomic industry, which is bound to be only for a comparatively short period of time, I think there is something wrong. I think it would be far more effective to go into an area like the north where the resources lie. If there is going to be a program of these incentives, surely it is better to go into these areas where we have the opportunity, the program and the resources. We did this in respect of the Pine Point railway. This was a partnership arrangement between the government, the railways and industry and it has been tremendously successful.
This is the sort of thing the government should be doing in the north. I think the time is very late when this should be done. I am sorry I have exceeded the time I had intended to take. My proposal is that when the Minister of Finance has brought down his Budget the debate well might be postponed to permit the subject matter of the Budget presentations, the fiscal and monetary policies which the government feels are necessary and adequate for the country for the next year, to be submitted to a committee before which would appear the advisors of the minister who have advocated these policies and before which also would appear others who do not agree with those policies. I think this would initiate in the country a real debate on and give us an opportunity to come to grips with the economic problems. This is something which is so essential and necessary.
I have sat through eight or nine Budget debates. This debate has been a good debate. However, this is the sort of thing we need
The Budget-Mr. Patterson rather than a debate in a vacuum, in a place where there is no conflict of ideas and no joinder of issue on the questions, the question of United States capital coming in here and the question of free trade. These are problems in which the people of this country are vitally interested. I think these things need to be brought out into the open, examined critically and considered thoroughly before the debate continues.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the course of the last election campaign I took the position that one of the greatest needs at the present time is responsibility in government. Because of the constant political campaigning which had characterized our parliaments and the ever present possibility of another election, I made the suggestion that it might be desirable to have a set term for parliament, such as four years, during which the only permissible occasion for an election would be on the defeat of the government on a straight want of confidence motion, the number of which would be strictly limited. I suggested that one such occasion would be the Budget debate, because we know the Budget is the main indicator of the monetary and fiscal policies of the government.
Personally I have refrained from supporting non-confidence motions based on specific issues, but because I was opposed to the position taken by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) with reference to general monetary and financial policy I found myself last evening in the position of being compelled to register my protest by voting non-confidence in the present government. I did so because I believe the general trend of the Budget speech and the policies enunciated by the minister is not in the best interest of this nation. I should like to read the first point mentioned in the press release from the office of the Minister of Finance outlining the highlights of the Budget.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
The current economic boom, with rising demands pressing against available production capacity, presents a great challenge to Canada to manage our present prosperity and maintain a steady and sustainable rate of growth.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that contributions during the course of this debate have raised a serious question as to the extent and magnitude of the suggested boom. It is true that many parts of the country and no doubt many citizens of the country are enjoying a very adequate share of the prosperity that is
April 22, 1966

The Budget-Mr. Patterson spoken of, but we dare not close our eyes to the fact that all is not as bright as the minister suggests.
For instance, I listened with a great deal of interest to the contribution to this debate of the hon. member for Kings (Mr. McQuaid). In the course of his presentation he gave a very dark and gloomy picture of the existing economic situation in his home province of Prince Edward Island. I am not saying that was overdrawn; I am not saying that conditions are not as dark as he suggested. I am just pointing out the fact that here was an hon. member who in presenting the conditions of his own province did not take the position that all was well and everything was bright and rosy. However, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that perhaps in some instances such conditions are not altogether caused by a lack of recognition on the part of the rest of Canada of these particular situations. I am not going to say they exist because the policies enunciated by the federal administration are not adequate to meet the needs, but I would suggest there may be a possibility that provincial policies are not adequate to meet the demands at the provincial level.
Therefore I would suggest that in some of these areas people might give consideration to electing a Social Credit government which might be able to present a picture that is a little brighter, because where Social Credit has formed the administration conditions are very bright and encouraging and those areas are developing better and faster than any other part of our great nation. I throw that out, Mr. Speaker, as a suggestion. Perhaps if conditions are not right and things are not going well, if the economic situation is dark, these people had better look around for some other type of administration which can bring a degree of prosperity and assistance to areas in difficult straits.
I should like to re-emphasize the fact that provincial administrations do have a great deal to do with national progress and development because if policies are not adequate and effective in the various provinces then, of course, the revenue accruing to the federal administration with which to fulfil its responsibilities is also lacking. Therefore I would again point to my own province of British Columbia and the neighbouring province of Alberta and bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the economic and financial policies that are being applied there. I say they are resulting in a measure of development and


progress that is unequalled in any other part of this great country of Canada.
I have mentioned that there are areas of this country which are not enjoying the boom to which the minister has alluded. There are also various classes of our citizens who are not enjoying the affluence of which we speak. There has been considerable discussion this session of the plight of old age pensioners. Suggestions have been made, amendments have been proposed and speeches have urged the implementation of further assistance to our senior citizens to bring their income up to a level at which they can live with a measure of dignity and decency. But the attitude of the government has been that it is not in an economic or financial position to provide this assistance.
I suggest that if our economic and financial situation is not adequate to meet the needs of our senior citizens and others at that particular income level, there is something wrong with the administration of our national affairs if we are enjoying such a boom that we have to put on the brakes. I have spoken of the old age pensioner. I could refer to federal superannuates, I could speak of our veterans, I could call to your attention, Mr. Speaker, all those living on fixed or low incomes. I suggest that these people are not enjoying that standard of living commensurate with an affluent society, one in which the government feels it essential to brake and slow down our development. Therefore I suggest that not all areas or citizens of this country would support the claim that Canada is enjoying an unprecedented boom.
I should like to have referred to a number of specific matters in detail but because there has been agreement to limit our contributions in order that as many members as possible may take part in the debate this afternoon I shall refer to them only briefly. Some of the documents to which I intended to refer will be set aside and I shall refer only to some specific situations. First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the tight money policy being implemented by the federal government at this time. I do not know whether they would call it a tight money policy; they refer to it as slowing up a little, taking your foot off the gas to spread the boom out a little so it will last longer. But I would suggest that in the final analysis it is a tight money policy which will have very serious effects upon the development of this nation.
It has been brought to our attention that there is a severe shortage of money for
April 22, 1966

construction purposes. I have a telegram at hand from the Ontario Council of the National House Builders Association referring to the desperate situation created by the complete lack of N.H.A. mortgage funds, which is critical to the housebuilding industry. The members of this association strongly urge immediate government action to re-establish the program of direct N.H.A. mortgage loans in all areas. I have received other communications from builders' associations and those engaged in the construction industry pointing out the fact that this policy will have a very serious effect upon the whole construction industry and will also spread into a great many related and allied trades.
The suggestion is that there is a shortage of skilled labour. I should like to call attention to the April issue of the "Canadian Builder". After referring to the effect taxation is having on the industry, this publication refers to the alleged shortage of manpower and states at page 34:
The fact is that the short-sightedness of the immigration policies of various governments in this country has created this situation.
I would suggest that rather than slowing up construction and our economy because there may be a shortage of labour, we should see to it that sufficient labour is brought in to augment our labour force in order to carry through the tremendous program of development and progress that is possible in Canada at the present time.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
Continuing along this line, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the fact that we in the Social Credit party have advocated for a number of years that the Bank of Canada provide facilities and capital to assist our municipalities in their programs for the provision of services to their people. I should like to re-emphasize this this afternoon because I believe it is important and pressing. I suggest that without something like this our municipalities are not going to be able to carry forward their programs and meet the challenge of their growing communities. We have suggested that a municipal development bank be established as a branch of the Bank of Canada. Money would be provided at a very low rate of interest, perhaps covering the cost of administration or at least a very low rate of interest, in order that municipalities might provide the facilities that are required in their communities.
The Budget-Mr. Patterson
I thought for a while that the government was moving in the right direction by establishing the municipal development assistance fund or loan fund. They saw fit, however, to cut it back just when it was getting nicely into operation. I say that the municipal authorities are very unhappy about the decision of the government in this respect.
We think, Mr. Speaker, of the entire debt structure of Canada. Reference has been made to this by other speakers. At the moment the service charges on our national debt require $1,100 million annually. I suggest this is something that ought to cause great concern. 1 was interested, however, to note that the government is moving in a direction we Social Crediters have advocated for a number of years, namely, that the Bank of Canada take over the national debt, assume responsibility for it and work toward its liquidation. The Bank of Canada has purchased some bonds in the past.
I cut out of the Ottawa Citizen for April 18, 1966, an advertisement with reference to an issue of $325 million non-callable government of Canada bonds. The advertisement states that the Bank of Canada has already agreed to acquire a minimum of $50 million of the new bonds, open as to maturity. I suggest that this is a move in the right direction. There ought to be more of it because it is much better to pay the interest back to the Consolidated Revenue Fund since that means in effect that we are getting our money at practically no interest. I therefore commend the minister and the Bank of Canada for this action. We would only urge that it be extended still farther.
I believe it was the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) who, speaking last night, asked this question: If the government cannot balance the budget in boom times, when can it be done? I believe this is a question of which the Minister of Finance should take cognizance and provide an answer. If we cannot meet our obligations now, if we have to continue borrowing and building up the national debt, further increasing the debt charges at this time when the minister says we are in such a boom we have to slow up, then when in the name of common sense are we going to be able to get to the place where we can balance our budget and operate this country on a business basis?
I should like to refer, Mr. Speaker, to the cost of living index. It has been pointed out
4186	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Patterson that the cost of living is constantly increasing. The Ottawa Journal for April 7 contained an article with this headline, "In The Last Six Months, Food Prices Up 6 Per Cent." We are told we have not reached the peak yet, that we can expect a continuing rise in the cost of living and in the prices of our products. I believe that this is one of the most distressing factors in our whole economy today.
I have received letters, as I am sure many members have, from old age pensioners who have gone into supermarkets, compared prices and found that the little bit of money they try to stretch to provide even the basic necessities of life is not sufficient to purchase enough for them to get by.

DEBATES	April 22, 1966
I am simply pointing out that the cost of living is constantly increasing and the ones who are getting hurt most are the ones who can bear it least. No attempt was made in this Budget to provide any of the assistance required. We talk about savings and investment. I am sorry that I am going on because I intended to be very brief but these interjections are interesting and provide some opportunity for a little digression.
However, in so far as savings and investment are concerned, I have an article here which I am not going to read. It is from the Ottawa Citizen for April 1, 1966. The heading is "Report Shows Canadians Can't Afford To Invest." The article goes on to say that Babson's estimates that a household with earnings of $7,000 a year after taxes spends 91 per cent on living expenses, leaving 9 per cent for accumulation. Of course, if you reduce that to the bracket in which many of our Canadian citizens live there is no money left for investment. In fact, the people cannot tighten their belts any more because they are so tight now the people would not get by if they tightened them any more.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I refer now to the income tax. The report which appeared in the newspapers following the introduction of the Budget stated that six out of ten would pay more taxes. Everybody knows that we have a social responsiblity in Canada to assist those who are unable to assist themselves. We have an obligation imposed by our need to have the government do for us collectively what we cannot do for ourselves individually. There is a limit financially, Mr. Speaker. You can kill the goose that lays the golden egg. I believe that is what is going to happen if the government maintains its trend of increasing taxes, overburdening the Canadian people and overburdening the taxpayers.
I have in my hand a letter from a young man who expresses deepest bitterness because the government is dictating to him how he is going to spend his money, implying that he has not enough brains to know how to spend it himself. I quote one brief paragraph:
Forgive me if I got carried away but I feel so strongly about this and other things that I am going to have to live with for many, many years. It seems that my future is being carefully plotted out for me while all that I can do is write letters and pray that I will still be able to have a choice of where I will work and what I will do as time progresses. Sometimes I feel as if I want to break out and scream as I watch my decisions made for me by a government that believes that I haven't got enough brains to take care of myself.
April 22, 1966

I believe that brings out the picture very clearly. It shows that some people think that the government says to people: You have not got enough sense to know how to spend your own money; we are going to look after it for you. Therefore the whole structure that is being erected is a denial of the rights of the individual to look after himself and to live his life as he wants to live it.
With regard to taxation policy the minister hides behind the fact that the Carter Commission has not made its report. I think the government is hiding behind that report. There is no reason why it could not proceed to bring about relief to the Canadian people. Instead, it hides behind this report, making excuses. We hope that the commission will report quickly.
In view of the agreed limitation of debate and the courtesy extended by the house, I am going to conclude my remarks at this time. I do, however, register my strong exception to the policies followed by the government in dealing with some of our national problems and I object to the lack of any policy with respect to other issues of concern to the Canadian people.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me to congratulate you on your appointment as Speaker of this house. Everyone to whom I have spoken about you has praised your ability to handle difficult situations quickly, fairly and in an orderly manner.
I should like to thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) for presenting to this house a wise budget which fits the needs of the hour. The task of the government is to sustain the longest economic expansion in Canadian history and therefore we must have some restraint in our expansion to safeguard the continued growth of our economy. Time Magazine says:
This inflation-dampening budget earned a round of editorial and business approval.
I have checked the reaction of many of my constituents to this budget. One farmer said, "It did not hurt us, but Joe Greene sure saved our hide". A businessman said that he thought it was a budget that should check inflation and it did not hurt him too badly; he had expected an increase in personal taxes but he did like the 5 per cent refundable corporation tax. "Over all" he said, "this budget should trim inflation." I quote from an article in the Globe and Mail of April 5:
Economists generally like the refundable tax, which they regard as perhaps the most sophisticated
The Budget-Mr. Lind instrument of economic control that Ottawa has devised in a generation.
What does the ordinary man on the street think of this budget? I have talked to many on this point. They generally agreed that it did not hurt us and they expected the minister to check the inflation so why not clip those who can afford it? This judicious rebalancing of income tax will help to check or dampen inflation without disturbing the underlying uptrend in business.
I would like to suggest to hon. members and the government that they consider the image of this parliament and the business life of our country by considering for a moment the meaning and value of integrity. Colton once said:
Nothing more completely baffles one who is full of trick and duplicity than the straightforward and simple integrity in another.
The Oxford Dictionary defines integrity as "wholeness, uprightness, and honesty". The World Book Dictionary defines it as "honesty and sincerity". A man of integrity is a respected man and I believe it is our duty as members to be respected men and women. I believe that a re-dedication to those principles for which our forefathers and predecessors stood is necessary if we are not to slip back into the morass of a totalitarian state. Popularity and public acclaim are not the measure of a man. What should matter most to hon. members is that we conduct the business of our country with integrity. We should, when necessary, operate as a trust, doing the unpopular thing when it is in the best interest of the country so to do and always foregoing self-interest. As the business leaders of Canada entrusted with the affairs of this nation, we must at all times exercise integrity.
Some hon. members may greet this suggestion with cynicism but it is not too difficult for the thinking person to see the practical values of integrity. It is both efficient and economical and although not always easy to practise its reward is serenity of mind.
I should like to suggest to the Minister of Finance and our government an area which I call the erosion of our tax base through business failures, namely, bankruptcies. Our government has and is doing something about this situation, but I urge them to speed up the process and save the consumer, the farmer, the businessman and corporation from the terrible loss through bankruptcies which, last year were in excess of $500 million in Canada.
4188	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Lind
Daily in our local papers we have been reading about the scandalous collapse of one of our largest finance companies. I quote from an article in the Globe and Mail of February 4, 1966:
Responsibility for the collapse of Atlantic Acceptance Corporation Ltd. last summer, rests entirely with a small handful of not-so-clever-but completely arrogant-scoundrels, thoroughly familiar with the bankruptcy game.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Some of the scandal took place in the constituency of Middlesex East. Just south of 401 highway-excuse me; it is known now as the Macdonald-Cartier Freeway-on one of the main access routes to London, Wellington Road, is situated a famous shopping area known as Treasure Island. It was here that a lawyer and a London businessman set up Wildor Holdings Ltd. and, either intentionally or unintentionally, they, along with some of the principals in Atlantic Acceptance Corporation, proceeded to demonstrate how to turn the corners in business. According to the reports in the London Free Press, even before the British Mortgage and Trust Company had advanced the moneys under the first mortgage, a particular gentleman had his hand in the bread basket and received some $10,000 for processing the first mortgage. It appears to me that a certain London lawyer seems to have been rather closely connected with this transaction.
Then suddenly we find the principals of Treasure Island running out of moneys to complete the project, so the British Mortgage and Trust Company foreclosed under their rights as the first mortgagee. At that time there was outstanding over $335,000 in mechanics liens against Treasure Island by local firms and supply houses. In addition, there were several thousands of dollars in judgments against this property. The businesses concerned, which had trusted the integrity of these London businessmen and this lawyer, now find themselves with their equity completely wiped out.
The next thing we know is that Treasure Island is refinanced by Atlantic Acceptance Corporation. The people of our area naturally expected some new principals. But who are the principals? None other than Wildor Holdings Limited. The same London lawyer and businessmen are involved. They finish Treasure Island and negotiate with a local farmer for an additional two acres of land on which to build an arena. Under the guiding hand of this London lawyer they pay $6,000 for the two acres of land. But the property is

DEBATES	April 22, 1966
registered in the name of a relative of the London lawyer and is immediately sold to Wildor Holdings Ltd. for a mere $100,000.
Someone cut the $94,000 melon. It would be interesting to know who got a slice of this melon. Maybe the Minister of Finance could bring this to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson). I should like to press for a thorough investigation into this Treasure Island debacle. Many of my constituents suffered while these fellows hid behind the law.
I could go on talking about this fraud at great length. I ask hon. members to realize that this happened right under the noses of our provincial authorities. Something is very much wrong with the administration of our laws when these rascals can fleece the small businessman and not be brought to justice. Let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, that this happened in my riding and not in the province of Quebec. Allow me to quote from an article in the Globe and Mail of February 4, 1966:
Many of the characters in the Atlantic affair were old hands in the bankruptcy game. We recognize a number of the individuals, and had known of their association with Atlantic for a long time.
Many of these names were also associated with British Mortgage and Trust, in which a large number of my constituents also lost heavily along with constituents of the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith). Several of our older residents lost much of their savings and stocks last July before Ontario finally stepped into the picture and guaranteed the depositors. I urge the minister to consider bringing all near-banks and other such institutions which are taking deposit moneys under one single act so that we can in future avoid this rocking of our financial structure. The president of Clarkson and Company says: "Atlantic is probably the worst blow the free enterprise system in Canada has suffered in many years." I do hope that these individuals are pursued and brought to justice.
Let us look at some of the statistics on bankruptcies. In 1946 defaulted liabilities in Canada totalled $6 million, with 278 estates in bankruptcy. These jumped in 1950, the first year after the 1949 amendments to the Act, to 1,303 bankruptcies and $25 million of defaulted liabilities. If we admit the principle of the relation of cause to effect, we must conclude that the 1949 amendments resulted in an immediate increase of 500 per cent in the number of bankrupt estates and 400 per cent in the liabilities of bankruptcies in 1950 compared with 1946.
April 22, 1966

The operation was becoming so profitable that this increase continued, and at the end of 1963 the amazing figures were reached of 3,678 estates in bankruptcy and $193,700,000 in defaulted liabilities. It is a truly devastating torrent, and this during the most prosperous years experienced by Canada.
Confronted by this plague, certain associations and groups prepared some 47 briefs and presented them to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin).
In reply to these briefs and to the suggestions made by these associations, it was stated in judicial circles that the Bankruptcy Act was well thought out and protected the creditors provided they used it when they believed their rights to have been encroached upon. Without pretending to know more than these lawyers, I do maintain that when creditors are systematically victimized by these organized frauds they are not at all protected by the Act. On the contrary, they are being duped. The responsibility for pursuing these bankrupts falls on the shoulders of the creditors who have already lost very heavily. It also becomes the responsibility of the creditors to inform the Superintendent of Bankruptcy.
What are the duties of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy? The answer is given in Section 3 of the Act. After speaking about his appointment by the Governor General in Council, subsections 2 and 3 contain provisions as to the powers and duties of the superintendent. The part most interesting to creditors is paragraph (f) of subsection 3 which says that the superintendent shall-
-receive and keep a record of all complaints from any creditor or other person interested in any estate and make such specific investigations with regard to such complaints as the superintendent may determine.
It must be noted that if the Act in using the word "shall" binds the superintendent to do a certain thing, the same act gives him complete freedom when it uses the word "may", because if the superintendent does not have the appropriate staff or the appropriate funds then there is physical incapacity. I strongly recommend that the phrase "may determine" he changed to "must determine" to do away with this distinct weakness in the present Act, and I urge this house to consider immediately the new amendments to the Bankruptcy Act found in Bill S-17 of the Senate. Surely the urgency of this matter is very obvious to hon. members when we consider the losses to individuals, businessmen and corporations during the last ten years.

The Budget-Mr. Lind
In 1955 the number of estates in bankruptcy was 1,795. In 1960 this number had risen to 2,828. Here are the figures for subsequent years: in 1961, 2,659; in 1962, 3,190; in 1963, 3,678; in 1964, 3,606; in 1965, 5,003. I would draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that in 1946 there were 278 estates in bankruptcy whereas last year there were no less than 5,003 estates in bankruptcy. Between 1955 and 1966 there was an increase of some 3,208 bankruptcies. Most surely, part of this increase must have arisen as a result of planned bankruptcies.
What about the defaulted liabilities over the period from 1955 to 1965? In 1955 total defaulted liabilities amounted to some $53 million. In 1960 the total was $174 million. In 1961 it was $116 million; in 1962, $149 million; in 1963, $194 million; in 1964, $203 million. In 1965 it had risen to $392 million, a figure which does not include the loss amounting to more than $100 million sustained by over 40 businesses which were put into receivership following the collapse of Atlantic Acceptance Corporation. I consider these figures conclusive evidence that the bankruptcy racket does erode the tax base, and that these losses must ultimately be borne by you and by my constituents, as well as causing many innocent victims to suffer injustice.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
I believe the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) has given the reason why changes in the act are necessary when he stated as reported at page 2211 of Hansard:
I am also very anxious to explain to members of the committee the difficulty which the minister has in trying to administer a very complicated, awkward, and obsolete act, in trying to deal with what has become sophisticated and, I understand, organized crime in the field of bankruptcies.
I urge that a committee study Bill S-17 and that immediately this committee make recommendations to the house for changes in this obsolete Bankruptcy Act. The Minister of Justice on March 4 outlined some of the changes to the act. These changes could return some integrity to business, instead of such scandalous reports as these.
In summary, I urge you to look at the figures. In 1946 the number of estates in bankruptcy were 278, with a total liability of $6 million. In 1949 the Bankruptcy Act was revised, and immediately bankruptcies jumped, so that in 1950 there were 1,303 estates in Bankruptcy with a total liability of $25 million. This bankruptcy operation was

April 22, 1966
The Budget-Mr. Lind booming-and by the end of 1963 the number of estates in bankruptcy had risen to the amazing figure of 3,678 with a total liability of $194 million. This is a devastating amount.
In 1964 the Attorney General of Quebec instigated a special investigation squad to check into bankruptcies, and under the present laws was able in 1965 to reduce bankruptcy liabilities in Quebec by some $5 million, and the number of estates in bankruptcy by 123.
What happened in Ontario, which also had a special squad of investigators, according to the deputy attorney general of Ontario? Ontario's bankruptcies jumped from a total liability in 1963 of $84 million to a total of $260 million in 1965, and this does not include the over $100 million caused by the Atlantic Acceptance debacle. Sir, this Atlantic Acceptance scandal has rocked the financial structure of our country; therefore I urge the Attorneys General of all provinces to take action to stop this fantastic situation.
We all know that the administration of justice is a provincial responsibility, but I urge co-operation with the provinces to investigate all fraudulent activity, in fact every estate in bankruptcy. Bankruptcy liabilities in Ontario increased by over 325 per cent from 1964 to the end of 1965, and in Canada by over 88 per cent. Therefore I urge the Minister of Finance, along with the Minister of Justice, to help the provinces fight this scandalous monster, bankruptcy.
